stories.delivered_paragraph: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the company has “never advocated” banning open-weight AI models, responding to criticism that its closed-model business wants tighter control over the technology. Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, Google, OpenAI and others have backed a letter opposing premature restrictions, prompted partly by Chinese models nearing frontier performance at much lower cost. Amodei instead urged targeted safeguards for models with genuinely dangerous capabilities.

stories.delivered_paragraph: X has begun rolling out X Money in the U.S. to Premium and Premium Plus subscribers, expanding Elon Musk’s effort to turn the social platform into an “everything app.” The service offers a digital wallet, free person-to-person transfers, Apple Wallet support and a metal Visa card; it advertises up to 6% annual yield for eligible users. The launch moves X into a heavily regulated payments market after an invite-only beta and prior consumer-safety concerns.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned companies that hand all their data, prompts and AI work to one proprietary model provider risk “outsourc[ing] your thinking” and ultimately may not survive. Speaking on CNN, he said businesses should retain the metadata generated when using models so they can train their own systems or use open models later. The comments position data control and AI gateways as strategic safeguards, not merely technical infrastructure.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Investors are concerned by a report that Nvidia could backstop an OpenAI data-center lease, potentially creating the largest arrangement of its kind. One analyst told MarketWatch the structure could revive a troubling tech-bubble-era habit, in which suppliers help finance customers’ purchases and make demand appear stronger. The issue matters because Nvidia’s AI-chip sales are central to the spending boom, and intertwined financing could make its durability harder for investors to judge.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to let it enforce parts of President Donald Trump’s March order restricting mail-in voting, 99 days before the November midterms. A federal appeals court voted 2-1 on Saturday to keep a block in place, saying the order could bring unprecedented federal involvement in state-run elections and risk voter disenfranchisement. Twenty-three states argue the president lacks authority to impose the rules, setting up an urgent election-law test.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Seattle police now believe at least three people fired guns during Sunday’s shooting at the Bite of Seattle festival near the Space Needle, revising their initial account of two shooters. Three people were killed and at least four injured, including a two-year-old; one 15-year-old suspect is in custody, one suspected shooter died at the scene, and police are seeking at least one more. The revised account underscores the scale of the continuing investigation at a major tourist event.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Small businesses including spice seller Burlap & Barrel, watch retailer Collective Horology and toymaker Learning Resources filed new lawsuits challenging Trump administration tariffs that took effect last week. The measures impose 10% or 12.5% duties on imports from more than 60 economies the administration says did not adequately block goods made with forced labor. The suits extend a wider court fight after earlier challenges had already overturned or cast doubt on other Trump tariff programs.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Senior U.S. officials believe economic pressure may ultimately damage Iran’s government more than the recent bombing campaign, as reports point to worsening shortages, including gasoline, inside the oil-rich country. Trump paused U.S. strikes after 13 consecutive days and said Iran sought talks, a claim Tehran denied. Mediators from Oman, Qatar and Pakistan are pursuing a durable ceasefire, with proposals involving traffic through the Strait of Hormuz now part of the negotiations.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Shots were fired at the U.S. consulate in Toronto for the second time this year, and the suspect remained at large after police pursued a vehicle in a high-speed chase. Three people were arrested after a similar attack in June, but the report does not establish whether the incidents are connected. The repeat targeting of a U.S. diplomatic site is likely to intensify the investigation and security concerns around the consulate.

stories.delivered_paragraph: CNBC’s China Connection newsletter says the accelerating AI race is reshaping U.S. and Chinese national priorities beyond the two countries’ long-running tariff disputes. The focus is increasingly on technology leadership and the policies needed to support it, as competition heats up this summer. That shift matters because AI policy may now influence trade, industrial strategy and national-security decisions more directly than conventional tariff negotiations alone.

stories.delivered_paragraph: A Los Angeles judge ruled that singer D4vd, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, will stand trial on murder charges over the death of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez. Prosecutors allege Burke stabbed and dismembered her after years of sexual abuse; her remains were found last September in a Tesla registered to his address. Burke, 21, has pleaded not guilty, with arraignment set for August 31 and trial expected within 90 days afterward.

stories.delivered_paragraph: New Line Cinema won a bidding war involving at least 10 parties for “Jealous People Are Ugly People,” a horror project from Greek-British filmmaker Theo James Krekis. Krekis will adapt and direct the feature from his BBC-commissioned short, which follows a man whose jealousy of a friend’s success feeds a supernatural force. The competition reflects Hollywood’s growing appetite for digital-era horror creators after recent breakout genre hits drew major box-office attention.

stories.delivered_paragraph: “Obsession” star Michael Johnston is in early talks to join Universal’s fourth “The Mummy” film, alongside returning leads Brendan Fraser and Rachel Weisz. Radio Silence directors Matt Bettinelli-Olpin and Tyler Gillett are set to make the sequel for an October 15, 2027 release. Johnston’s potential casting follows the unexpected success of “Obsession,” a $750,000 independent film that grossed more than $458 million worldwide, turning him from a relative unknown into a sought-after actor.

stories.delivered_paragraph: A federal magistrate judge ordered Donald Trump’s trust to provide some business financial records to the BBC as the network defends against the president’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit. Judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett granted the BBC’s request only in part, limiting the subpoena’s scope. The ruling gives the broadcaster access to evidence potentially relevant to damages while preventing the discovery fight from becoming an unrestricted examination of Trump’s finances.
